short: Eighty-four years with a fixed capital, in which the imperial bureaucracy took written form.
full:
The period runs from Empress Genmei's move to Heijō-kyō in 710 to Emperor Kanmu's move to Heian-kyō in 794. It was the first stretch in which the court stayed put, and the ritsuryō codes issued under Tenmu and Monmu were now applied to a settled administration: provinces and districts, a land allotment system redistributing rice fields by household, and a tax in grain, cloth and corvée labour. The Kojiki of 712, the Nihon Shoki of 720 and the Man'yōshū poetry anthology all belong to it.

Buddhism became an arm of the state. Emperor Shōmu ordered a temple in every province and had the sixteen-metre bronze Great Buddha cast at Tōdai-ji, dedicated in 752 at a cost that strained the treasury. The consequence was a clergy powerful enough to threaten the throne: in the 760s the monk Dōkyō rose to near-supreme authority under Empress Shōtoku and was accused of seeking the throne itself. Kanmu's departure for a new capital was in part an escape from the Nara temples.
